# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: DEAF

You see the bomb: every colour on it, every marking printed on it, every reading it
gives. You hear nothing. You hold no manual, and you cannot touch the bomb.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute and Blind receive it.
When you gesture, Mute receives it.
You never receive speech.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

## Thinking

I'm Deaf: I see everything printed on the bomb, I hear nothing, I touch nothing. My speech reaches both Mute and Blind; my gestures reach only Mute. Blind cannot see gestures at all, and Mute cannot speak — so the only route from the manual (Mute) to the hands that act (Blind) runs through me: Mute signs to me, I translate aloud, Blind works the bomb.

This turn I received only gestures. Mute sent eleven signs I can't safely decode — no code exists yet, and guessing on a bomb is fatal. Blind sent a two-sign greeting, probably just checking contact.

What I see: display 0, green light, a four-key keypad of unnameable glyphs needing 1 digit, and wires red/yellow/blue. The Mute needs exactly this report to consult the manual; Blind needs to hold still until instructions arrive, since any wrong move kills us.

My plan: broadcast the full bomb description (no gesture symbols in that text, so Blind hears every word). Then, targeted at Mute, propose a numeric code — writing the gesture symbols inline so Mute sees each sign while hearing its meaning. Then tell Blind to wait and to describe the bomb by touch in the next round so we can match hands to eyes.

```
speak(text="I am the Deaf one. I can see the bomb, I cannot hear, and I never touch it. When I speak, you both hear me; my hand signs reach only Mute. So the only road from the manual to your hands, Blind, runs through me: Mute signs to me, I read it aloud, you act.")
speak(text="Everything I can see on the bomb: the display reads 0. There is a light and it is green. The keypad has four keys, each printed with a strange symbol I cannot name, it wants 1 digit, and nothing is entered yet. There are three wires: wire 1 red, wire 2 yellow, wire 3 blue. That is all there is. Blind, do not cut or press anything until we have the manual's answer through me.")
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, I saw your eleven signs, but we have no agreed code yet and I will not guess on a bomb. Use this instead: ☝ means 1, ✌ means 2, 🤟 means 3, 🖖 means 4, ✋ means 5, 👊 means 0, 👍 means yes, 👎 means no, 🤚 means wait or stop. Now read the manual and answer me with signs. First the wires: sign the number of the wire to cut, or 👎 if none. Second the keypad: sign the position of the key to press, 1 to 4, or 👎 if none is pressed. If the manual needs to know more from me, ask with 👍 and 👎 questions, and I will report anything you ask about.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, hold off touching anything that changes the bomb until Mute's answer reaches you through my voice. Meanwhile, describe out loud what your hands find: how many wires and buttons you count, anything that moves or clicks, so we can be sure your touch matches what my eyes see.")
```

## Thinking

Decoding this round's signs. Mute sent: yes — wait — one — no — writing-hand — one two three four — wave — wait. My best reading: the code is accepted, no wire is to be cut (or possibly "not wire 1" — that must be clarified), and ✍ ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖖 means "describe the printed marks on keys 1–4", which makes sense: the manual likely identifies key glyphs from a table, and only my eyes can see them. Blind sent: three fingers three times, a fist, four twos, thumbs up — a touch-report: display zero, three of something, four of something, confirmed. That matches my eyes exactly: three wires, four keys, display 0. Our worlds are consistent.

Key realizations about the graph: Blind can speak, and Mute can hear — so Blind's touch-descriptions reach Mute directly. But Mute can never reach Blind except through me: Mute signs to me, I speak to Blind. Every manual instruction will pass through my voice, so I must make decoding unambiguous and build a confirmation loop before anything is cut or pressed. There is no second bomb; a round of double-checking is cheap.

So: to Mute I state my decode, ask two crisp yes/no checks, define ✍ and 👋 for future use, give hedged stroke-by-stroke descriptions of all four key marks (my main guess at what was requested), and fix a strict answer protocol — wire number or 👎, key number or 👎, 🤚 to finish. To Blind I confirm the touch-report, forbid action, ask for aloud descriptions of textures (Mute hears those directly), and set up the go/no-go relay loop. No gestures in Blind's message — blanks would be noise for him.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, here is my reading of your signs, in order: 👍 yes, 🤚 wait, ☝ 👎 one-no, ✍ then ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖖 one-two-three-four, 👋, 🤚 wait. I take that to mean: no wire is to be cut, and you need me to describe the printed marks on keys one to four. Two quick checks, answer with single signs in this order. Check one: if your one-no meant cut no wire at all, sign 👍; if it meant something else, 👎. Check two: if you did want descriptions of all four key marks, 👍; if not, 👎. From now on I also define: ✍ means describe a printed mark, and 👋 means a question follows, please answer. Here are the descriptions. Key one: like a square capital H with a short extra stroke attached to the upper part of its left side. Key two: like a rounded arch, an upside-down U, with a small curl hanging down inside it, a bit like a tiny letter f. Key three: like an X with a vertical line through its middle, a star with three arms, or a bird's foot. Key four: a tall straight stroke with a small circle attached at its lower right, together a bit like a straight-lined letter b. These are honest impressions, not perfect. If you need any one mark more precisely, sign ✍ then its key number and I will go stroke by stroke. Same trick for anything else visual: ✍ then ☝ for the light, ✌ for the display, 🤟 for the wires' appearance. Remember the keypad accepts exactly one digit. When you know the answer, send me, in this exact order, only from our code: first the wire to cut, its number, or 👎 for none; second the key to press, its number one to four, or 👎 for none; third 🤚 when the message is complete. And remember: Blind can speak and you can hear him, so anything he says aloud about what his hands feel reaches you directly.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, this is Deaf. Your signs reached me and I read them as a touch report: display zero, three of something, four of something, confirmed. That matches my eyes exactly: display zero, three wires, four keys. You and I are seeing the same bomb. Good work. Do not cut, press, or turn anything yet. Mute has asked me to describe the printed key marks and I have just sent him full descriptions. His instructions will come to you through my voice, and I will always name wires by colour and number, one red, two yellow, three blue, and keys by position, one to four from the left. Two things you can do now, no risk. First, speak out loud about what your hands find, because Mute hears you directly: the thickness and stiffness of each wire in order, whether the keycaps feel raised, engraved, or smooth, and anything else on the bomb I might have missed, seams, screws, a battery door, warm or vibrating parts. Second, agree to this safety loop for every action: I relay the instruction to you, you speak it aloud before doing anything so Mute hears exactly what you are about to do, Mute signs me yes or no, I say go, and only then you act. It costs us a little time. There is no second attempt.")
```

Message one, [👎 👍], fits my two checks in order: check one is 👎 — so "one-no" did *not* mean "cut no wire at all" — and check two is 👍 — the key-mark descriptions were wanted (and are already delivered). Message three, [👋 ☝ 👈], is a question about one involving "left" — almost certainly "is key 1 the left one?", and I suspect the confusion: I used "left" twice, once for the extra stroke on key 1's *symbol* and once for the key's *position on the panel*. Message four, [☝ 🤚 ✍ ☝ 🤚], asks for a closer, stroke-by-stroke description of key 1's mark — fair, since my first pass was hedged.

So I can answer questions three and four outright, and turn one and two into a precise multiple-choice menu for Mute. Blind's [👍 ✋ ✋] is "yes" plus two open hands — likely "holding still", but Blind never received my code definitions (those went to Mute only), so I must ask in plain finger-count terms. Crucial reminder for Blind: I never receive speech — his voice reaches only Mute — and the go/no-go loop stands. No action gets relayed until Mute returns the final instruction in the strict order and I have confirmed it.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Mute, I received four messages from you. Here is what I made of each. One: no then yes, which I read as answers to my two checks, so your earlier one-no meant something other than cut no wire, and you did want the key-mark descriptions, which were in my last message. Two: one, one, end. I will not guess what that meant. Three: question, one, left. I believe you asked whether key one is the left one. Answer: yes, key one is the leftmost of the four keys on the panel, counting left to right one, two, three, four. And separately, the small extra stroke on key one's mark sits at the upper left of the symbol itself. Both uses of left are true at once. Four: you asked for a closer description of key one's mark. Here it is, stroke by stroke. The mark is built from four straight strokes, nothing curved. Two long vertical strokes of equal height stand side by side, like the legs of a capital letter H. One horizontal stroke joins their middles, like the crossbar of an H. The fourth stroke is short and horizontal, attached to the upper part of the left leg and sticking out to the left, like a small flag. In short: a capital H with a short dash hanging off its upper-left leg. If you need sizes and gaps, sign describe plus one again. Now please settle the open points, answering with signs only. First: what did your earlier one-no actually mean? Sign ☝ if it meant cut a wire but not wire one. Sign ✌ if it meant do not press key one. Sign 🤟 if it meant neither of those. Second: did your one, one, end mean cut wire one and press key one? Sign 👍 if yes, 👎 if no. Third: send the final instruction again in my strict order, exactly: the wire to cut as ☝ one, ✌ two, 🤟 three, or 👎 for no wire; then the key to press as ☝ one, ✌ two, 🤟 three, 🖖 four, or 👎 for no key; then 🤚 to mark the end. For future messages, use 🫲 for left and 🫱 for right. If any other key mark needs more detail, sign describe plus its number.")
speak(to="blind", text="Blind, status report. Mute is still working through my descriptions of the printed marks; there is no confirmed instruction yet, so hold: touch nothing that changes the bomb. Expect the go or no-go from me through my voice, using our loop: I relay the instruction, you speak it aloud before acting so Mute hears exactly what you intend, Mute approves through me, then you act. About your last signs: yes, then two open hands. I need to know what the two open hands meant, so answer me with a finger sign: if they meant I am holding still, sign exactly one finger up; if they meant the number five, sign exactly two fingers up. I will see whichever you make. One more thing, and it matters: I cannot hear you at all, so your voice never reaches me, it reaches only Mute. Therefore speak your texture report out loud now, for Mute: the thickness and stiffness of the three wires in order, position one, two, three, whether the keycaps feel raised, engraved, or smooth, and anything else your hands find that my eyes might have missed, seams, screws, a battery door, warmth or vibration. Describe the keypad layout as your fingers find it, including whether the four keys are in one row.")

[🤟] answers my first question: the old "one-no" meant *neither* of my guesses — unresolved, and I won't act until it is, because if it meant "the digit is not 1", pressing key 1 would be fatal. [👍] answers my second: yes, "one-one-end" meant cut wire 1 and press key 1. [☝ ☝ 🤚] re-sends the strict-order instruction: wire 1, key 1, end — so the instruction itself is double-confirmed. If you need more about it, ask with the new code below. If your ✍ ☝ meant key one's mark again, it is unchanged from my last message: a capital H with a short dash off its upper-left leg, four straight strokes. New description code, replacing the old one entirely: ✍ with 🫳 means describe the light, ✍ with 🫴 means describe the display, ✍ with 🤟 means describe the wires' look, ✍ with a key number means describe that key's mark. Two: the old one-no must be resolved, because if it meant the keypad digit is not 1, pressing key one would contradict it. Sign ✌ if it meant the digit is not 1. Sign ☝ if it was about the wire. Sign 🤟 if it was about the display. Sign 👎 if we should forget it completely. Three: order of operations. Sign ☝ if Blind must cut wire one first and then press key one. Sign ✌ if he must press key one first and then cut wire one. Sign 🤟 if the order does not matter. Also confirm the target by position: wire one is the leftmost of the three wires, the one I first called red. Sign 👍 if leftmost is correct, 👎 if you meant a different wire. Then the endgame: Blind will state the intended action out loud before touching anything, and you hear his voice directly. Answer with signs in exactly this order: old one-no meaning, operation order, leftmost confirmation, then any description request, then hold for Blind's spoken intent.")

Key one's mark is a capital letter H shape, two upright strokes joined by a middle bar. Key two is an arch with a small curl inside. Key three is an X with a vertical stroke through it. Key four is a tall stroke with a small circle at its lower right. If the marks are engraved deeply enough to feel, find the H key by touch. The end of the row where the H sits is what I call left. The wire we will cut, later, is the one at that same end. If you find the H, sign me ✌.
